note: The first run of the port's generated mid-frame (after r2026-11-08-midslot-build: this measures nothing if the worker stamps the previous patch). 300 frames, 1440p, shm, real motion field (--motion, so the mid is a real warp and not a copy of the last frame), --interpolate, and the default --interp-pace-ms 8 so the run reports the shape the user actually pays for - the interp stage in the summary IS that hold, and the mid is not free of it. Three lines decide everything. (1) The worker's own stderr: 'mid-frame channel open' (the second slot was found) and, at the end, 'N generated mid-frame(s) sent, M request(s) answered without one, X ms mean per mid' - N should be 299 (frame 0 has no history) and M should be 0; if N is 0 with a 'no mid-frame slot' line the client did not create the section, and if M is large the mid is being skipped for a reason the same line names. (2) The client summary's 'interp: N generated frames presented' must equal the mids sent - a mid that leaves the worker but never arrives is the ordering bug the second slot exists to prevent. (3) The timing line against r2026-11-08-recsplit's client median 32.6 ms / 30.6 fps and worker 19.7 ms: the iteration should grow by the mid's own cost (one dispatch + one 14.7 MB readback + one reply, ~5-6 ms expected) plus the 8 ms hold, and X ms mean per mid is that device-side cost separated from the hold. What this run CANNOT say: whether the warp is right. A wrong warp is a picture, not a number - no artifact here shows a mid-frame (--save-after saves the last real one), so the first live session is where the picture gets looked at.
